chapters.title: Chapter 3: Reading and Building a Cap Table

lessons.title: What a Cap Table Is and Why Every Investor Must Read One

children.text: Every concept from the first two chapters, share counts, fully diluted ownership, CCPS, round prices, ends up in one document: the cap table. It is usually a single spreadsheet, and many angels never ask to see it. That is a mistake. In ten minutes, a cap table can tell you who controls the company, how much money sits ahead of you in an exit, whether the team is still motivated and whether anything has been promised that nobody mentioned in the pitch. This lesson teaches you to read one. The next lesson teaches you to build one.

body.text: A cap table is the company's ownership X-ray. It shows who owns what today, who has been promised what tomorrow and who gets paid first. A founder who cannot produce a clean one is telling you something important.

children.text: What Goes Into a Cap Table
A
cap table
lists every holder of every security, grouped by type. A good one has these columns.

markDefs.definition: Short for capitalisation table: a record of every security a company has issued or promised, who holds it, what they paid and what percentage it represents.

cells: Who you are in business with
Equity, Pre-Seed CCPS, Seed CCPS, options, warrants
Shares held or to be received
The numerator of every ownership calculation
Shows how the valuation has moved round by round
Share of all shares including promises
Economic ownership, the number that matters for value

children.text: Reading a Real-Looking Cap Table
NammaFarms Agritech Private Limited is a fictional Bengaluru startup connecting small farmers to restaurant buyers. Here is its cap table after a Seed round.

body.caption: NammaFarms cap table after the Seed round (illustrative)

children.text: Percentages are rounded to two decimals, so columns may add up to 100.01% or 99.99%. Issued capital is 7,30,000 shares (equity plus CCPS). Fully diluted capital adds the 80,000-share ESOP pool and 10,000 warrants, for 8,20,000.

body.title: NammaFarms fully diluted ownership by group (%)

children.text: Five Questions a Cap Table Answers
Who controls the company?
Founders hold 76.71% of issued shares, above the 75% needed for special resolutions. On a fully diluted basis they hold 68.29%, still well above 50%.
Do the founders still have enough skin in the game?
At 68% after two rounds, yes. Founders who are already below 50% at seed have little room left for Series A, B and C dilution.
How much money sits ahead of equity?
Both CCPS series carry a 1x preference, so ₹60 lakh plus ₹3 crore, a ₹3.6 crore preference stack, is paid before any equity holder in a sale.
How much ESOP is left to hire with?
50,000 unallocated options, 6.10% of the company. Too little and investors will demand a top-up that dilutes you. Lesson 3.3 covers this.
What is coming that is not yet shares?
10,000 warrants are listed. Always ask whether any convertible notes or iSAFEs are outstanding, because some cap tables leave them out until they convert.

stats.label: Preference stack
stats.context: Paid before equity in a sale

stats.label: Unallocated ESOP
stats.context: Room to hire before a top-up

body.title: Voting power today
body.prompt: Options and warrants do not vote until they become shares. Assume CCPS vote on an as-if-converted basis. What percentage of NammaFarms' issued shares do Priya and Arvind hold together? Answer to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Priya and Arvind hold 3,20,000 + 2,40,000 = 5,60,000 shares. Issued shares total 7,30,000. 5,60,000 ÷ 7,30,000 = 76.71%, enough to pass a special resolution on their own today, even though their fully diluted stake is 68.29%.

children.text: Red Flags to Look For

body.caption: Cap table red flags and why they matter

cells: A co-founder who left two years ago still holds 20%
Large stakes held by people no longer building the company reduce motivation and put off future investors
Little room for future rounds; founders may lose motivation or control too early
The company cannot hire senior talent without a pool top-up that dilutes everyone
An "advisor" or early backer with 8% for introductions
Value given away that does not build the business
A convertible note mentioned in the deck but not on the cap table
"We have promised our CTO 3%, it is just not documented yet"
Undocumented claims can become disputes and surprise dilution
Share counts differ from the MCA annual return
Either the cap table or the statutory records are wrong

body.text: A private company in India can have at most 200 members, excluding current and certain former employees. A startup that takes ₹2 lakh cheques from dozens of individual angels can clutter its cap table and edge towards that limit. This is one reason Indian angel platforms typically pool investors through a single SEBI-registered angel fund or AIF, which appears on the cap table as one holder.

body.title: Spot the biggest problem
body.question: You are reviewing a seed-stage cap table. Which of these should concern you most?
options: An ESOP pool of 8% with half already granted
A seed fund holding 15% through CCPS
A co-founder who left 18 months ago still holding 22% with no vesting or buyback
Two angels holding 1% each through equity shares
body.explanation: A 22% stake held by someone no longer working in the business is classic dead equity. It rewards someone who is not building the company, reduces the stake available to motivate the people who are, and is often a deal-breaker for Series A investors. The other three are normal features of a seed-stage cap table.

children.text: Verify the Cap Table Against Official Records
A cap table is a spreadsheet the company prepares. The statutory records are what the law recognises. Before investing, cross-check them.

body.title: Company cap table vs statutory records

columns.label: Company cap table
points: Prepared by the founders or their CA
Includes options, unallocated pool, warrants and convertibles
Shows fully diluted percentages and preferences
Can be out of date or optimistic

columns.label: Statutory records
points: Register of members kept by the company
Return of allotment (Form PAS-3) for every issue
Filed with the Registrar of Companies and viewable on the MCA portal for a fee

body.title: Name the basis
body.textWithBlank: A cap table that shows ownership as if every option, warrant and convertible instrument had already become equity shares is prepared on a fully ___ basis.
body.explanation: Fully diluted percentages show economic ownership once every promise is kept. Issued percentages show only shares already allotted.

body.title: The cap table review call
body.scenario: You are considering a ₹10 lakh cheque into a Chennai logistics startup. The founder shares this summary: Founder A 38% equity, Founder B 24% equity, Founder C (left the company last year) 18% equity, angels 12% CCPS, ESOP pool 0%, and "a ₹75 lakh convertible note from a family office, which isn't on here because it hasn't converted yet." On the call, the founder adds that the new Head of Sales "has been promised 2% once we close this round."
body.prompt: List the issues you see and what you would ask for before investing.
body.modelAnswer:
Issues:
1. Dead equity. Founder C left last year but holds 18%, more than all angels combined. Ask whether Founder C's shares had vesting, and whether a buyback or reverse vesting is possible.
2. No ESOP pool. With 0% reserved, the company must create a pool before or during the next round, diluting everyone including you.
3. Missing convertible note. ₹75 lakh will convert into shares, possibly at a discount or capped price. It must appear on a fully diluted cap table with an estimate of the shares it becomes.
4. Undocumented promise. A verbal 2% to the Head of Sales is future dilution with no agreement behind it.
5. The numbers only add up to 92%. Ask what makes up the other 8%.

Ask for:
1. A complete fully diluted cap table, before and after this round, including the note and the planned ESOP pool.
2. The shareholders' agreement terms on vesting and leaver provisions for founders.
3. The convertible note terms: discount, valuation cap and maturity.
4. Written confirmation of all equity promised to employees or advisors.
5. The latest MGT-7 and PAS-3 filings to verify share counts.

body.title: Your cap table reading routine
steps: Ask for the cap table on both an issued and a fully diluted basis, before and after the round.
Check that percentages add to 100% and the share counts tie to the latest MCA filings.
Calculate the founders' combined fully diluted stake.
Add up every liquidation preference to find the preference stack.
Check the ESOP pool: total size, granted and unallocated.
Ask directly about convertible notes, iSAFEs, warrants and verbal promises.
Look for dead equity and passive holders with large stakes.

cards.definition: A record of every security a company has issued or promised, who holds it, what they paid and what it represents.
The total of all liquidation preferences that must be paid before equity holders in an exit.
A significant stake held by someone no longer contributing to the company, such as a departed co-founder.
The company's statutory record of its shareholders, which the law treats as the official record of ownership.
The annual return filed with the Registrar of Companies, which includes shareholding details.
The maximum number of members a private company can have, excluding current and certain former employees.

points: A cap table lists every security issued or promised, with holders, share counts, prices, amounts invested and ownership percentages.
Read both issued percentages, which drive voting today, and fully diluted percentages, which drive economic value.
A cap table tells you who controls the company, how motivated the founders are, how big the preference stack is and how much ESOP is left.
Watch for dead equity, over-diluted founders, missing ESOP pools, hidden convertibles and verbal promises.
Private companies are limited to 200 members, which is why angel platforms usually pool investors into one vehicle.
Always verify the cap table against PAS-3, MGT-7 and the register of members.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment or legal advice. NammaFarms and the other startups and people described are fictional. Startup investments are high risk and illiquid and can result in the loss of your entire capital. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before investing.
